thread.previously: The 2023 women's quota waits on a census and delimitation. On 17 April 2026 the 131st Amendment, enlarging the Lok Sabha to up to 850 seats on 2011 census data, failed to get two-thirds. On 26 November 2026 the Centre announced a special sitting: Lok Sabha 30 November, Rajya Sabha 2 December, possibly to 3 December. An amended Delimitation Bill is likely; its text is unpublished. Congress alleges 'Op Lotus' poaching; a CPI MP says his party will reject an unchanged bill.
thread.changed: The Cabinet cleared the new bills on 27 November. Unlike April's bill, which removed the freeze, this one raises every state's seats by 50% and keeps state shares fixed until 2051.

stories.headline: Cabinet clears 50% Lok Sabha rise, seat-share freeze to 2051
stories.question: How would freezing state seat shares until 2051 change India's Lok Sabha and women's quota?
stories.dek: Every state would get 50% more Lok Sabha seats, so no state's share of the House changes until 2051. The bigger House is meant to make room for the one-third women's quota.

so_far.text: In 2023 the 106th Amendment promised women one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats. The catch was timing: the quota starts only after a census and a delimitation (the redrawing of seats). On 17 April 2026 the 131st Amendment failed. It would have enlarged the Lok Sabha to up to 850 seats on 2011 census data. The vote was 298 for and 230 against, short of two-thirds. Special sittings of Parliament were then set: Lok Sabha from 30 November, Rajya Sabha from 2 December.

what_happened.text: On 27 November 2026 the Union Cabinet cleared a new Constitution Amendment Bill. It raises every state's Lok Sabha and Assembly seats by 50%, to give effect to the 33% women's reservation. It also freezes each state's share of Lok Sabha seats until 2051, a 25-year freeze. The Indian Express published what it says is the full text of the Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, listing 850 Lok Sabha seats. A separate Delimitation Bill uses 2011 census data.

steps.text: Since 1976 the split of Lok Sabha seats between states has been frozen at 1971 census levels.
Re-sharing seats on new population figures would shift power between states; southern chief ministers wanted the freeze kept 25 more years.
A uniform 50% rise gives every state more seats while each state's share of the House stays the same.
The bigger House is meant to make room for the 33% women's reservation.
It is still a Constitution Amendment, so it needs two-thirds of MPs voting, which April's bill did not get.

history.text: The story starts in 1976. The 42nd Amendment, passed under Indira Gandhi's government, froze each state's number of Lok Sabha seats at 1971 census levels. The aim was to encourage population control. A state that slowed its population growth would not lose seats for it. In 2001 the 84th Amendment extended the freeze until the first census after 2026. Seat boundaries inside a state could still be redrawn, but the split of seats between states stayed fixed. That deadline set up the fight over the 2026 bills. In March 2025 a Joint Action Committee of southern chief ministers demanded another 25-year freeze based on the 1971 census. It included Tamil Nadu's M.K. Stalin and Telangana's Revanth Reddy. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge made a similar demand of Prime Minister Modi. Meanwhile, the 2023 women's quota could not start until delimitation happened, so it became tied to the seat question. In April 2026 the 131st Amendment tried to settle both. It would have removed the freeze and enlarged the House on 2011 census data. It failed on 17 April. The new bill takes the opposite route: it keeps every state's share fixed.

lesson.concept: How a uniform seat rise keeps every state's share
lesson.big_idea: A state's power in the Lok Sabha depends on its share of seats, not the raw number. If every state's seats rise by the same percentage, the numbers grow but every share stays exactly the same.

steps.title: Count versus share
steps.text: A state's count is its number of MPs. Its share is that count divided by the whole House. The share decides how much the state weighs in any vote.

steps.title: Population re-sharing moves power
steps.text: Delimitation can share seats by population. Since 1976 the split between states has been frozen at 1971 census levels, to encourage population control. Unfreezing would move shares around.

steps.title: Same rise, same share
steps.text: If every state grows by 50%, the state's seats and the total House both grow by 50%. So the fraction is unchanged. The new bill proposes this, with shares fixed until 2051.

steps.title: Room for the women's quota
steps.text: The 2023 law reserves one-third of seats for women. Grow a House by 50%, reserve one-third, and the seats left open to all equal the House's size before the rise.

example.setup: Imagine a small parliament of 100 seats. State A has 20 seats and State B has 80. Suppose a fresh population count would give State A only 15.

lines.label: A's current share
lines.note: Its weight in every vote.

lines.label: Re-share by population
lines.note: What unfreezing could do to A.

lines.label: Uniform 50% rise
lines.note: Every state grows by the same percentage.

lines.label: A's new share
lines.note: Share unchanged, just as under a freeze.

lines.label: Women's one-third
lines.note: Reserved for women in State A.

lines.label: Open seats left
lines.note: Exactly State A's 20 seats before the rise.

example.result: A uniform rise lets every state gain seats without any state losing weight. With a one-third women's quota, the seats left open to all equal each state's number before the rise.

apply.text: Now the news. The new bill gives every state 50% more seats; one summary says Karnataka, which currently has 28, would go to 42. Its share would stay fixed until 2051. One-third of 42 is 14 seats for women, leaving 28 open seats, equal to its current count. News18 framed the bill as the government's attempt to turn the tables after April's defeat.

practice.q: Say a state currently has 40 Lok Sabha seats. After a 50% rise and a one-third women's quota, how many seats are reserved, and how many stay open?
practice.answer: 50% of 40 is 20, so the state gets 40 + 20 = 60 seats. One-third of 60 is 20 seats reserved for women. 60 − 20 = 40 seats stay open to all, equal to its 40 seats before the rise.

stories.headline: Goyal says India-US trade deal close as US proposes 25% tariff
stories.question: Is India about to seal a US trade deal that cuts its proposed 25% tariff?
stories.dek: Piyush Goyal says an India-US deal is close. It would mean a 17% US tariff, not the proposed 25%. Both exceed the 10% baseline as of 27 November 2026. Nothing is signed.

so_far.text: In February 2026 the US Supreme Court struck down much of Trump's broad tariff programme, which rested on emergency powers. That left Indian goods on a baseline US tariff of 10%. By 26 November 2026 the US had proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, citing excess manufacturing capacity. India would face 25%, or 17% if it signs a deal. Vietnam would face 35%, or 20% with a deal. China would face 20%. A February 2026 framework had promised India 18%, but a formal deal was never signed.

what_happened.text: On 27 November 2026, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said the India-US trade deal is close to culmination. He said the "process and pathway" for finalising it is taking shape, The Hindu reported. Reuters, Bloomberg and Business Standard also reported him saying the deal is nearing completion. Bloomberg noted that he spoke after the US proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods. It is not yet known when the deal will be signed. The deal decides whether Indian goods would face the proposed 25% US tariff or the lower 17%.

steps.text: After the Supreme Court ruling, the US proposed new tariffs on 14 partners, citing excess manufacturing capacity.
India's proposed rate drops from 25% to 17% if it signs a deal, so signing becomes the way to pay less.
Rivals face similar terms: Vietnam 20% with a deal, China 20%, and Bangladesh, Cambodia and Indonesia 18%.
At 17%, Indian goods could undercut those rivals in the US; at 25%, they would cost more.
So India has a reason to close fast, but keeping dairy, poultry, rice and wheat out remains a sticking point.

history.text: The story starts in February 2025, when Modi and Trump launched India-US trade talks. The two countries already had long-running disputes over agriculture, digital trade, medical devices and market access. In April 2025 the US announced a 26% "reciprocal" tariff on India. In late August 2025 that became 25%, plus a further 25% penalty for buying Russian oil. That made 50% in total. On 6 February 2026 the two sides announced an interim framework, an outline agreement made before a full deal. It cut the US tariff on Indian goods from 50% to 18%. It also removed the oil penalty, because India committed to stop buying Russian oil. In return, India was to scrap or cut tariffs on US industrial goods and many farm items. Goyal aimed to sign a formal deal in March 2026, but it was not signed. Also in February 2026, the US Supreme Court struck down much of the broad tariff programme, which rested on emergency powers. That left Indian goods on a 10% baseline. By 26 November 2026 the US had proposed new tariffs on 14 partners, citing excess manufacturing capacity. India was offered 25%, or 17% with a deal. That is why the unsigned deal suddenly matters again.

lesson.concept: How tariff gaps decide who wins US orders
lesson.big_idea: A tariff is a tax a country adds to imports at its border. For an exporter, what matters is not only its own rate, but how it compares with rivals selling the same goods.

steps.title: A tariff is a border tax
steps.text: When a US company imports goods, it pays a tax called a tariff at the border. It is a percentage of the goods' value. A 10% tariff on a $100 shipment adds $10.

steps.title: The buyer sees a higher price
steps.text: The importer usually passes some or all of that tax on to its customers. So the higher the tariff, the dearer the goods look next to the same goods from elsewhere.

steps.title: Each country gets its own rate
steps.text: The US proposal gives each country its own rate. India faces 25%, or 17% with a deal. Vietnam faces 35%, or 20% with a deal. China faces 20%.

steps.title: The gap moves orders
steps.text: A US buyer comparing two similar shirts looks at the price after tariff. A gap of even a few percentage points can shift orders to the cheaper country.

steps.title: A deal has a price
steps.text: A deal lowers your rate, but you give something back. Under the February 2026 framework, India was to cut tariffs on US industrial goods and many farm items. It wants dairy, poultry, rice and wheat kept out.

apply.text: So when Goyal said on 27 November 2026 that the deal is close, this gap is at stake. At 17%, India's goods would beat Vietnam's and China's 20% and the 18% for Bangladesh, Cambodia and Indonesia. At 25%, India would pay more than all of them, unless Vietnam fails to sign.

practice.q: Say a US buyer imports a $20 bag from Bangladesh at 18% and the same bag from India. What does each cost if India signs, and if it doesn't?
practice.answer: Bangladesh: 18% of $20 = $3.60, so $23.60. India with a deal: 17% of $20 = $3.40, so $23.40, slightly cheaper. India without a deal: 25% of $20 = $5, so $25, dearer by $1.40.

Goyal says the deal is close; it means 17%, not 25%, both above the 10% baseline.

stories.headline: SAP weighs 10,000 job cuts as IBM ends most visa sponsorship
stories.question: Why is SAP weighing 10,000 job cuts, and why is IBM ending visa sponsorship?
stories.dek: SAP is reportedly weighing at least 10,000 job cuts to reshape its business for AI. IBM is ending most US visa sponsorship in consulting, after US pressure on work visas.

so_far.text: In 2024 SAP restructured 9,000–10,000 roles, mostly through voluntary exits and retraining, at a cost of about €3 billion. On 19 September 2025, Donald Trump signed a proclamation adding a one-time $100,000 fee to new H-1B work-visa petitions, up from about $1,500. A federal judge ruled the fee unlawful on 8 June 2026. In October 2026 the US suspended firms including Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS and Microsoft from a programme letting H-1B workers seek green cards.

what_happened.text: On 26 November 2026, Bloomberg reported that SAP is weighing cutting at least 10,000 positions, about 9% of its global staff, to reshape its software business for the AI era. It is a plan under consideration, not a confirmed announcement. SAP has asked product development, engineering and sales teams to find possible reductions. People familiar said earlier attempts to introduce AI products faced problems. Separately, IBM said, in reports published on 10 November 2026, that it will stop sponsoring US work visas and green cards for most roles in IBM Consulting, its largest division. It said its use of these programmes had shrunk for years.

steps.text: SAP wants its software business reshaped for the AI era, so it is reviewing which roles it still needs.
Salaries are paid every year, so cutting roles frees money that can be moved to new priorities like AI.
People familiar told Bloomberg that SAP's earlier AI product attempts faced problems; it has asked product, engineering and sales teams to find cuts.
In the US, the Trump administration raised pressure on visas: a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions and suspensions from a green card route.
IBM says its visa use had shrunk for years, so it is dropping a process it relied on only modestly.

history.text:
This story has two roots. The first is SAP. In June 1972, five former IBM engineers, including Dietmar Hopp, Klaus Tschira and Hasso Plattner, founded it in Germany. So SAP began with IBM people. It started public trading on 4 November 1988, and between 2012 and 2014 it bought SuccessFactors, Ariba, Hybris and Concur.

The second root is the US H-1B visa, which lets employers hire skilled foreign workers. The Immigration Act of 1990, signed on 20 November 1990, created it with a yearly cap of 65,000. After temporary rises, the cap returned in 2004 to 65,000, plus 20,000 for holders of US advanced degrees. Indian outsourcing firms such as TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant and HCL became top users. In 2021, half of the top 30 H-1B employers were outsourcing firms.

Then both roots began to shift. In January 2024 SAP announced a restructuring of about 8,000 roles. In July 2024 its chief financial officer, Dominik Asam, raised that to 9,000–10,000. It cost about €3 billion, which showed SAP would pay a large one-time sum to reshape its workforce. On 19 September 2025, Donald Trump put a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, up from about $1,500. A federal judge ruled the fee unlawful on 8 June 2026. In October 2026 the US suspended firms including Infosys, TCS and Microsoft from a route to green cards. In November 2026, IBM ended sponsorship for most of its consulting roles.

lesson.concept: How restructuring trades a one-time cost for yearly savings
lesson.big_idea: Cutting roles costs money once, for exit pay and retraining, but saves salaries every year. If yearly savings repay that cost quickly, the company moves the freed money to new priorities like AI.

steps.title: Salaries repeat every year
steps.text: A worker's pay is a cost that comes back every year, not once. For a software company, staff pay is usually a big regular cost. Remove a role, and that yearly cost goes too.

steps.title: Cutting has a one-time price
steps.text: Ending a role is not free. A company pays exit packages, runs voluntary programmes and retrains people. SAP's 2024 restructuring of 9,000–10,000 positions cost about €3 billion, mostly through voluntary programmes and retraining.

steps.title: Payback: cost divided by saving
steps.text: The payback period is how long the yearly savings take to repay the one-time cost. You find it by dividing the one-time cost by the yearly saving. A shorter payback makes a cut easier to justify.

steps.title: The freed money gets moved
steps.text: Restructuring means reshaping, not just shrinking. Money freed from old roles can pay for new ones. SAP's reported plan aims to reshape its software business for the AI era.

steps.title: Not every move is a cost sum
steps.text: Some company changes have other stated reasons. IBM says it is ending most consulting visa sponsorship because its visa use had shrunk for years. Reports say the move follows US pressure, including a $100,000 H-1B fee; how much each factor mattered is not known.

Now Bloomberg reports SAP is weighing at least 10,000 more cuts, about 9% of staff, and has asked product, engineering and sales teams to find reductions. IBM's move is different: it is ending visa sponsorship, citing years of shrinking visa use.

practice.q: Suppose a firm cuts 50 roles costing ₹10 lakh a year each, and each exit costs ₹20 lakh once. What is the payback period?
practice.answer: Yearly saving: 50 × ₹10 lakh = ₹5 crore. One-time cost: 50 × ₹20 lakh = ₹10 crore. Payback: ₹10 crore ÷ ₹5 crore = 2 years. After that, the firm saves ₹5 crore every year.

scenes.say: Step 1: salary har saal repeat hoti hai, toh ek role hatane se ek saalana kharcha hat jaata hai. Step 2: cut karne ki ek one-time keemat hoti hai. SAP ke 2024 wale round mein lagbhag 3 billion euro lage. Step 3: payback period yaani woh one-time cost, saalana saving se divide.

scenes.say: Step 4: restructuring ka matlab hai naya roop dena, sirf chhota karna nahi. Bacha hua paisa naye kaam mein lagta hai. Step 5: har kadam sirf cost ka hisaab nahi hota. IBM kehta hai ki woh sponsorship isliye band kar raha hai kyunki uska visa use saalon se ghata. Reports ise US visa pressure se jodti hain. Kis wajah ka kitna asar tha, yeh pata nahi.

scenes.say: Chaliye ek example lete hain. Maan lijiye ek software company mein 1000 staff hain. Har ek ka kharcha 20 lakh rupaye saal ka. Company 9 percent cut karti hai, yaani 90 roles. 90 guna 20 lakh, yaani 18 crore rupaye ki saalana bachat. Ab maan lijiye har exit ka ek baar ka kharcha 30 lakh hai. Toh total hua 27 crore.
scenes.speak: चलिए एक example लेते हैं। मान लीजिए एक software company में 1000 staff हैं। हर एक का ख़र्चा 20 लाख रुपये साल का। Company 9 percent cut करती है, यानी 90 roles। 90 गुना 20 लाख, यानी 18 करोड़ रुपये की सालाना बचत। अब मान लीजिए हर exit का एक बार का ख़र्चा 30 लाख है। तो total हुआ 27 करोड़।

scenes.say: Ab payback. 27 crore ko 18 crore se divide kijiye, aata hai dedh saal. 5 saal mein company bachati hai 90 crore. Isme se 27 crore ka kharcha ghataiye, toh 63 crore rupaye naye kaam ke liye free ho jaate hain.
scenes.speak: अब payback। 27 करोड़ को 18 करोड़ से divide कीजिए, आता है डेढ़ साल। 5 साल में company बचाती है 90 करोड़। इसमें से 27 करोड़ का ख़र्चा घटाइए, तो 63 करोड़ रुपये नए काम के लिए free हो जाते हैं।

stories.headline: Spain's Hernández de Cos picked to lead the European Central Bank
stories.question: Who is Pablo Hernández de Cos, and how will he steer the ECB after Lagarde?
stories.dek: Euro-area leaders backed the Spanish central banker on 26 November 2026. He is seen as a moderate dove, but he will chair a committee, not rule it alone.

so_far.text: The European Central Bank (ECB) sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro. Christine Lagarde has led it since 1 November 2019. She will step down on 7 February 2027, before her term ends. On 29 October 2026, António Costa, president of the European Council, began the process to choose her successor. The final contest was between Pablo Hernández de Cos of Spain and Klaas Knot of the Netherlands. In mid-November, EUobserver reported that Paris and Berlin appeared to have struck a deal favouring Hernández de Cos.

what_happened.text: On 26 November 2026, euro-area leaders gave Pablo Hernández de Cos the nod to be the next ECB president, Bloomberg reported. The Guardian, CNBC and The New York Times also reported that he had won. He beat Klaas Knot of the Netherlands in the final contest. He will be the first Spaniard to lead the ECB. Euronews calls him a consensus figure and an orthodox economist with a civil-service career. He has run the Bank for International Settlements, a bank for central banks, since 1 July 2025. He will succeed Lagarde, who leaves on 7 February 2027.

steps.text: Choosing an ECB president is a package deal: leaders also share out other Executive Board seats between big countries.
Two seats open soon: Isabel Schnabel leaves in January 2027 and chief economist Philip Lane in May 2027.

history.text:
The ECB was founded on 1 June 1998, replacing the European Monetary Institute. When the euro arrived on 1 January 1999, the ECB took full powers to set one interest rate for all euro countries. The big test was the debt crisis. On 26 July 2012, ECB president Mario Draghi pledged to do 'whatever it takes' to preserve the euro. A bond-buying plan called OMT followed in September 2012. That showed markets the ECB was ready to act. Next came the era of very cheap money. The ECB cut its main rate to 0.05% in September 2014. It began quantitative easing, creating money to buy bonds, in January 2015. Lagarde took over from Draghi on 1 November 2019. In July 2022, with euro inflation at 8.9%, the ECB began raising rates. On 21 July 2022 it also launched the Transmission Protection Instrument, a tool to stop the gap between countries' borrowing costs from blowing out.

Meanwhile, Hernández de Cos rose through the system. Born in Madrid in 1971, he joined the Bank of Spain's research department in 1997. Spain's Rajoy government proposed him as governor on 28 May 2018, days before it fell to a no-confidence vote. He served from June 2018 to June 2024. From 2019 he also chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which sets global rules for banks. On 1 July 2025 he became general manager of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), succeeding Agustín Carstens. In January 2026, after a US criminal probe of Jerome Powell, he helped rally central bank chiefs behind a 'full solidarity' statement led by Lagarde.

lesson.concept: How a central bank committee sets interest rates
lesson.big_idea: The ECB president does not set rates alone. A committee votes. The president frames the debate and builds a majority, so who sits at the table matters as much as the president's own views.

steps.title: Rates are the main tool
steps.text: A central bank's main tool is its interest rate. Raising it makes loans dearer, so people and firms borrow and spend less, and prices rise more slowly. Cutting it does the reverse and supports growth and jobs.

steps.title: Hawks and doves
steps.text: A hawk worries most about inflation and leans towards higher rates. A dove worries more about growth and leans towards cuts. Il Foglio called Hernández de Cos a 'moderate dove' and Klaas Knot a pragmatic 'hawk'.

steps.title: A committee decides
steps.text: At the ECB, rates are set by the Governing Council. It is made up of the six-member Executive Board, which includes the president, plus the governors of the euro countries' national central banks.

steps.title: The president steers; seats matter
steps.text: The president chairs meetings, shapes the proposal and speaks for the decision, but needs a majority. So seats matter: Isabel Schnabel leaves the Executive Board in January 2027 and Philip Lane in May 2027.

example.setup: Imagine a made-up rate committee of 10 members. Four lean dove, including the chair, who wants a rate cut. Four lean hawk. Two sit in the middle. Assume a cut needs a simple majority.

lines.label: Votes for a cut
lines.note: The chair starts with their own camp.

lines.label: Majority needed
lines.note: Assume a simple majority wins.

lines.label: Gap to close
lines.note: The chair must win both middle members.

lines.label: One middle member refuses
lines.note: No majority, so the chair must compromise, say on a smaller cut.

lines.label: A hawk seat goes dove
lines.note: Now one middle vote is enough.

example.result: The chair's view sets the direction, but the outcome depends on winning the middle and on who fills empty seats. One seat change can turn a lost vote into a win.

apply.text: So when euro-area leaders chose Hernández de Cos, they chose the chair, not the whole committee. Il Foglio calls him a moderate dove. Euronews expects him to side with hawks except on rates, where he argued for cuts in 2024. With Schnabel and Lane leaving in 2027, the seat deals France and Germany struck will shape the room he steers.

practice.q: Same 10-member committee, but now five lean hawk, three lean dove (including the chair) and two sit in the middle. Can the chair pass a cut?
practice.answer: A majority still needs 6 votes. The doves have 3. Even if both middle members join, 3 + 2 = 5. That is one short. The chair must win over at least one hawk, or settle for a smaller step or no change.

check.why: The president chairs and steers, but the Governing Council decides. The mix of members decides what can win a majority.

stories.headline: First run of days above 2°C does not break Paris limits
stories.question: What does a week of global temperatures above 2°C mean for the Paris goals?
stories.dek: For six or seven days in November 2026, the world ran more than 2°C above its 1850–1900 average. Paris counts 20-year averages, so no limit is broken. The rising trend is the real warning.

so_far.text: The Paris Agreement aims to hold global warming well below 2°C and to try for 1.5°C. Both limits are measured against the 1850–1900 average. The author of an analysis in The Conversation says long-term, human-caused warming is already near 1.5°C. During 2026 an El Niño grew. El Niño is a warm phase of the Pacific Ocean. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) said El Niño conditions were present during India's monsoon, which ended about 13% below normal. NOAA projections suggested the El Niño could become very strong and last into winter 2026–27.

what_happened.text: Preliminary data from the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service show global temperatures stayed more than 2°C above the 1850–1900 average for several days in a row in November 2026. Nature World News counts six days, from 18 to 23 November, the first such run on record, peaking at 2.24°C on 23 November. The Financial Times counts seven days, peaking at 2.25°C. On 23 November the world was also 1.34°C above the 1991–2020 average for that date, the largest gap on record. Forecasts suggested similar heat for several more days. All figures are preliminary and may be revised.

steps.text: Human emissions have already lifted long-term warming to near 1.5°C above the 1850–1900 average.
A strong El Niño, a warm phase of the Pacific Ocean, is adding extra heat on top.
Together they pushed daily global readings past 2°C for six or seven days from 18 November.
But Paris limits count long-term averages of about 20 years, so one hot week does not breach them.
The warning is the trend: 2026 may set a record, 2027 is likely hotter, and 1.5°C could pass by 2030.

history.text:
The story starts with a baseline. Scientists use the 1850–1900 average temperature as the 'pre-industrial' baseline. The Paris Agreement measures its goals against it: well below 2°C, and ideally 1.5°C. Paris looks at long-term averages, usually over about 20 years, not single days.

Scientists also compare each day with a more recent normal, the 1991–2020 average. In November 2023 one day ran 1.15°C above that normal. That stayed the record until November 2026. On 22 July 2024 the world had its hottest day ever in absolute terms, and that record still stands. Global temperatures rise and fall through the year with a seasonal cycle. So November's record is a record gap from normal, not the hottest absolute day.

In 2026 an El Niño grew. By June, NOAA projections suggested it could become very strong and last into winter 2026–27. Some scientists expected a 'super' event, but that was a projection, not an outcome. In India, the IMD cut its monsoon forecast from 92% of the long-period average in April to 90% in late May. The monsoon ended near 87%. The IMD said El Niño would dominate October to December.

Underneath it all, human-caused warming had reached about 1.5°C. El Niño's heat came on top of that. From 18 November 2026, daily global readings went above 2°C for the first time in a run of days.

lesson.concept: How Paris limits are measured: averages, not days
lesson.big_idea: A reading 'above 2°C' is a gap from a chosen average. Paris counts that gap over about 20 years, so a few hot days barely move it. A rising trend does.

steps.title: A gap, not a reading
steps.text: Climate scientists report an anomaly: how far the global temperature sits above an average for the same date. So '2°C' means 2°C warmer than that average, not a thermometer reading of 2°C.

steps.title: The baseline changes the number
steps.text: On 23 November 2026 the same day was 2.24°C above the 1850–1900 average but 1.34°C above the warmer 1991–2020 average. The heat was the same, but two baselines give two numbers.

steps.title: Paris uses the old baseline
steps.text: The Paris Agreement aims for well below 2°C and tries for 1.5°C, measured against 1850–1900. It refers to long-term averages, usually over about 20 years, not single days.

steps.title: Short spikes barely move averages
steps.text: A 20-year average covers over 7,000 days. A few hot days are a tiny slice of that, so they hardly shift the result. What shifts it is one warm year after another.

steps.title: Why the trend still matters
steps.text: Human-caused warming is already near 1.5°C, and El Niño adds more on top. 2026 may tie or set the hottest-year record, 2027 is likely hotter, and the world may pass 1.5°C as early as 2030.

example.result: Even a full year at 2°C lifts the 20-year average only from 1.5°C to 1.525°C. A single hot week adds about 0.0005°C. Breaching Paris takes many warm years, not one spike.

apply.text: So the six or seven days above 2°C in November 2026 are, on their own, a tiny slice of a 20-year average, and the Paris limits are not breached. The worry is step 5: warming already near 1.5°C, a possible record in 2026, a likely hotter 2027, and 1.5°C passed as early as 2030.

practice.q: Same 20 years, but assume half the years run 1.5°C above 1850–1900 and half run 2.0°C. What is the 20-year average?
practice.answer: Ten years at 1.5°C: 10 × 1.5 = 15. Ten years at 2.0°C: 10 × 2.0 = 20. Total: 15 + 20 = 35. Average: 35 ÷ 20 = 1.75°C. Steady warm years move the average far more than one spike.

stories.headline: Brands shift $254 million of Bangladesh garment orders, mostly to India
stories.question: Is Bangladesh's turmoil sending garment orders, and political trouble, India's way?
stories.dek: On orders, yes for now. Brands moved about $254 million of orders out of Bangladesh in 18 days, mostly to India, factory owners say. The political pressure on India is still building.

so_far.text: Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's former prime minister, fled to India in August 2024. On 17 November 2025 a Bangladeshi tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia, and Dhaka formally asked India to hand her over. She plans to return home on 16 December 2026. Bangladesh's garment industry has its own trouble. On 1 November 2026 the government formed a Minimum Wage Board to set new pay. On 2 November, nearly 400 factories shut during wage protests.

what_happened.text: On 27 November 2026, Reuters reported as an exclusive that global fashion brands diverted about $254 million of orders from Bangladesh between 1 and 18 November. Factory owners said most of the orders moved to India. Business Standard reported that retailers including Zara and H&M diverted the orders amid labour unrest and rising costs, and that India emerged as the biggest beneficiary. Separately, Moneycontrol and India Today reported that Hasina supporters plan a 230-km human chain to Dhaka. The plan reportedly involves 9 border routes and 5 million supporters, possibly walking in from India.

steps.text: Garment workers in Bangladesh want the minimum wage raised to Tk 30,000 a month, up from Tk 12,500.
Wage protests shut nearly 400 factories on 2 November: 264 in Savar-Ashulia and over 150 in Gazipur.
In general, factory shutdowns delay deliveries, and brands with fixed selling dates try to avoid such delays.
Brands diverted about $254 million of orders on 1–18 November, amid unrest and rising costs, mostly to India, reports say.
Separately, Hasina plans to return on 16 December, and reports of marchers possibly coming from India pull India into Bangladesh's politics.

history.text:
The garment side of this story starts with pay. In 2023 and 2024, large numbers of Bangladeshi garment factories closed when workers demanded wages of around Tk 23,000 a month. So pay fights that shut factories were already a pattern.

The political side starts in August 2024. A student-led uprising ended Sheikh Hasina's 15 years in power, and she fled to India. From then on, Bangladesh's politics had a direct link to India.

On 17 November 2025, Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia, meaning without her being present. Dhaka formally asked India to extradite her, or hand her over. That turned a political split into a legal demand on India.

In December 2025, India's foreign ministry said it "completely rejects the false narrative" spread by extremist elements in Bangladesh. It said the interim government had not shared meaningful evidence. Hasina stayed in India and the request stayed open.

In November 2026 the wage fight came back. On 1 November the government formed a Minimum Wage Board to set a new pay structure by December. Workers want Tk 30,000 a month, up from Tk 12,500. On 2 November, nearly 400 factories shut. On 27 November, Reuters reported that brands had moved about $254 million of orders, mostly to India.

lesson.concept: Why buyers move orders when supply gets risky
lesson.big_idea: Fashion brands need clothes on fixed dates. When strikes or rising costs make a supplier country likely to deliver late, brands may move orders to a backup country, even if it costs a bit more.

steps.title: Brands buy far ahead
steps.text: Big fashion brands place orders months before clothes reach shops. Each order has a fixed delivery date tied to a selling season, such as winter or a festival.

steps.title: Price is not everything
steps.text: A brand weighs the cost per piece against the risk of late delivery. A cheap shirt that arrives after the season starts is worth much less, because it may sell only at a discount.

steps.title: Unrest raises the risk
steps.text: When factories shut, every closed day pushes delivery later. Rising costs squeeze a supplier too. In Bangladesh, nearly 400 factories shut on 2 November 2026 over wages, and costs are rising.

steps.title: Orders move to a backup
steps.text: Brands may then shift some orders to another country that can make similar goods on time. Reports say orders left Bangladesh amid unrest and rising costs, and factory owners say most went to India.

steps.title: Shifts can stick or reverse
steps.text: Once a brand has tested a new supplier, it may keep some orders there. Or it may return when wages settle and factories reopen. Nobody knows yet which will happen here.

example.result: Even a short shutdown can push a tight order past its deadline. A slightly dearer supplier that delivers on time then wins the order. This is how unrest can move orders across borders.

apply.text: Reports say Zara, H&M and others diverted about $254 million of orders between 1 and 18 November, amid labour unrest and rising costs, mostly to India. Wage protests shut nearly 400 factories on 2 November. The lesson shows how shutdowns can push buyers away, though the reports do not spell out each brand's reasons. Whether orders stay may depend on new wages due by December.

practice.q: Same brand, but the deadline is 65 days and the Dhaka shutdown lasts only 3 days. India still costs $5,000 more. Does the brand switch?
practice.answer: Dhaka plan: 60 days + 3 days closed = 63 days. The deadline is 65 days, so the shirts still arrive 2 days early. There is no need to pay $5,000 extra, so the brand most likely stays with Dhaka.

stories.headline: Election Commission website exposed voters' details and ID documents, Reuters finds
stories.question: What voter data did the Election Commission's website expose, and is it safe now?
stories.dek: Reuters found that the EC website let logged-in users pull up other voters' contact details and ID files. The flaw is fixed now, but nobody knows how many voters were exposed, or for how long.

so_far.text: The Election Commission (EC) runs India's voter lists and an online portal for voters. Since 2025 it has run a Special Intensive Revision (SIR), a fresh recheck of voter lists. Opposition parties say the SIR disenfranchised millions. The EC says it followed all rules. In October 2026 The Hindu reported on a civic-tech audit. The audit found that state election officials' access to certain voter details could be switched on or off centrally.

what_happened.text: On 27 November 2026 Reuters reported a flaw on the EC's website. It exposed voters' personal details and the ID documents they had uploaded. The exposed fields were name, phone number, email, date of birth and address. File paths to identity documents such as passports were also exposed. None of this showed on the main screen. It appeared in the browser's network traffic and was reached through a form reference number. Reuters wrote to the EC on 26 October and got no reply. On 26 November a spokesman said the IT division was examining the findings. The flaw was fixed hours later.

steps.text: When a voter books a call on the portal, their form gets a reference number. The browser then requests that form's details in the background.
Researchers said the server only checked that the user was logged in. It never checked whether the requested form belonged to them.
Reference numbers were predictable. So changing the number could fetch another voter's record, and bulk downloads could be automated.
All of this ran in background network traffic. Nothing looked wrong on screen, so a script could repeat it quietly.
The fix hid the sensitive fields. Researchers say that blocks abuse from now on, but it cannot undo any earlier copying.

history.text: Fights over India's voter list began long before the website. In 2002–03 the EC ran a 'special summary revision of intensive nature' in 20 states, with house-to-house checks. Under 2003 guidelines, people already on the roll faced citizenship checks only if someone objected. The privacy problem has a history too. In 2019 researcher Karan Saini found an exposure similar to the new one on the EC's voter search portal. That was an early sign that the EC's online services could leak data. In June 2025 the EC added a call-booking feature to its website. Reuters says this is where the new flaw sat. On 24 June 2025 the EC ordered an SIR in Bihar. The term itself appears to be new in 2025. Bihar's final list dropped about 47 lakh names, roughly 5.95% of electors. Phase II was announced on 27 October 2025. It cut electors in nine states and three union territories from about 50.99 crore to 45.81 crore. In November 2025 the DPDP Rules were notified. Under them, an organisation that suffers a data breach must report it and tell the people affected. On 27 May 2026 the Supreme Court upheld the EC's power to run the SIR. On 26 October 2026 Reuters sent the EC its findings and got no reply for a month.

lesson.concept: Why logging in is not the same as permission
lesson.big_idea: A safe website asks two questions: who are you, and is this yours? The EC portal asked only the first. So any logged-in user could fetch other people's records.

steps.title: Proving who you are
steps.text: Authentication means the website checks your identity, usually with a login or an OTP. After that, your browser carries a pass that it shows with every request.

steps.title: Checking what is yours
steps.text: Authorisation means the server checks, on every request, whether that record belongs to you. Researchers told Reuters that the EC server skipped this check and only confirmed the user was logged in.

steps.title: Records are fetched by number
steps.text: Each form has a reference number. Your browser asks the server for 'form number X' in background network traffic that never appears on the main screen.

steps.title: Predictable numbers make it worse
steps.text: If numbers run in order, anyone can guess the next one. A small program can then ask for thousands of them, one after another. Reuters says this made bulk downloads possible.

steps.title: The fix: check and hide
steps.text: The proper fix is an ownership check on every request. The EC hid the sensitive fields, and researchers say this blocks abuse from now on.

example.setup: Imagine a portal where forms are numbered in order, one after another. You log in to see your own form. Assume a small program can send 10 requests a second.

example.result: Logging in only proved who you were. Without the second check, one predictable number opened all the others. A simple program could then turn one leak into tens of thousands of records within an hour.

apply.text: Researchers told Reuters this is what happened on the EC website. The server checked login, not ownership, and the reference numbers were predictable. A Reuters reporter fetched his own ID this way. The fix hid the sensitive fields. But nobody knows how long the flaw existed or whether anyone used it. So 'safe now' does not mean 'safe before'.

practice.q: On the old, unfixed portal, a program sends 5 requests a second for 2 hours. How many forms could it try, and what would stop it?
practice.answer: First, 5 × 60 seconds = 300 a minute. Next, 300 × 60 minutes = 18,000 an hour. Then, 18,000 × 2 hours = 36,000 forms. Only an ownership check on every request would stop it, because each request for a form that isn't yours gets refused.

stories.question: How will RBI's new money mule rules and ATM fee limits affect your bank account?
stories.dek: From 1 July 2027 at the latest, banks can hold suspected fraud money in your account on their own. ATM cash rules now sit in one rulebook, with alerts on free-use limits.

so_far.text: A money mule is a bank account used to pass on stolen money from phishing and other scams. Owners are often recruited online through fake job ads. Some innocent accounts are hacked and used without the owner knowing. The Supreme Court asked the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to frame a standard procedure for temporarily holding money in cyber-fraud cases. The RBI published a draft on 11 September 2026. Separately, the RBI caps what banks may charge for ATM use beyond your free monthly transactions: ₹23 per transaction since 1 May 2025.

what_happened.text: On 27 November 2026 the RBI issued final rules on suspected money mule accounts. They cover six types of bank, from commercial banks to urban co-operative banks. Banks must follow one uniform, time-bound standard operating procedure. They may, on their own initiative, place temporary debit holds on suspected mule or cyber-fraud amounts or accounts. They then lift the holds in coordination with police, while sparing genuine customers inconvenience. The rules apply from 1 July 2027, or earlier if a bank adopts them sooner. The same day, the RBI merged 17 circulars on ATM and card-machine cash withdrawals into one rulebook. Banks must alert customers about their free-transaction usage.

steps.text: Scammers pass stolen money through mule accounts, whose owners are often recruited via fake job ads, so the trail is hard to follow.
Each extra hop or cash withdrawal makes the money harder to trace and recover, so speed decides whether victims see it again.
The Supreme Court asked the RBI for a standard procedure, so that every bank acts fast but in the same fair way.
The final rules let banks hold suspect amounts on their own, under a time-bound procedure meant to spare genuine customers.
Separately, ATM rules sat across 17 circulars. One rulebook plus usage alerts should make charges easier for customers to track.

history.text:
The ATM side of this story starts in 2012. An RBI committee noted that the interchange fee last changed in August 2012. That is the fee your bank pays another bank when you use its ATM. Customer charges last changed in August 2014. For years after that, neither moved.

In June 2021 the RBI raised the interchange fee from ₹15 to ₹17 per financial transaction, such as a withdrawal. It went from ₹5 to ₹6 for non-financial ones, such as a balance check. Both changes applied from 1 August 2021. The cap on what customers pay beyond free transactions then rose from ₹20 to ₹21 from January 2022. It rose again to ₹23 from 1 May 2025. By 2026 the rules were spread across 17 circulars, and the RBI merged them on 27 November 2026.

The fraud side is newer. Money muling is an old trick: scammers move stolen money through other people's accounts so it is hard to trace. The Supreme Court asked the RBI to write a standard procedure for temporary debit holds in cyber-fraud cases. The RBI's draft of 11 September 2026 proposed four things. Flagged transactions of ₹1,000 or more could be held. Customers would get notice and 20 days to explain. Holds would be capped at 60 days unless police directed otherwise. Whole accounts would be frozen only as a last resort. After feedback, the RBI changed the draft and issued final rules on 27 November 2026.

analogy.text: Think of a security guard at a building gate. The guard stops one suspicious parcel for checking instead of locking the whole building, and everyone else keeps coming and going. The parcel is the suspect money; the building is your account.
analogy.breaks: A guard can open the parcel at once. A bank often needs police help to decide, so a genuine customer may wait weeks.

for_you.text: From 1 July 2027 at the latest, your bank can hold a suspect credit in your account on its own. Never let anyone use your account, even for a 'job'. At ATMs, expect alerts on how many free transactions you have used. Beyond free limits, the known cap is ₹23 per transaction. It is not yet confirmed whether the new rulebook changes free limits.

lesson.concept: How a bank debit hold on suspect money works
lesson.big_idea: A debit hold lets a bank stop suspect money from leaving an account, while money can still come in. The aim is to catch fraud money before it vanishes, without punishing genuine customers.

steps.title: Where stolen money goes
steps.text: Scammers rarely keep stolen money in their own accounts. They pass it through mule accounts. These are often run by people recruited through fake job ads, or they are innocent accounts hacked without the owner knowing.

steps.title: Speed decides recovery
steps.text: Each hop to another account, and each cash withdrawal, makes the money harder to trace. Once it leaves the banking system as cash, recovery gets much harder. So a bank has to act quickly.

steps.title: A debit hold, not a freeze
steps.text: A debit hold stops money leaving an amount or an account; money coming in still works. The final rules let banks place such holds on their own, under one uniform, time-bound SOP (standard operating procedure).

steps.title: Clocks protect the customer
steps.text: The September draft set clocks. Flagged transactions of ₹1,000 or more could be held. The customer gets notice and 20 days to explain. Holds end within 60 days unless police direct otherwise. The final text may differ.

steps.title: Release, with police
steps.text: Banks lift holds in coordination with police, and they must spare genuine customers inconvenience. The draft also required each bank to set up a complaints system and resolve complaints within 30 days.

It can hold the suspect amount on its own, follow one time-bound procedure and lift the hold with police. practice.q: Priya has ₹20,000 of her own. A flagged ₹8,000 credit arrives and is held. Then her ₹15,000 salary comes in. How much can she spend?
practice.answer: A hold blocks money going out, not money coming in. Total balance: ₹20,000 + ₹8,000 + ₹15,000 = ₹43,000. Held: ₹8,000. Usable: ₹43,000 − ₹8,000 = ₹35,000. Her salary is not affected.

stories.headline: Spain votes: could Vox enter government and end Sánchez's rule?
stories.question: Could Spain's 29 November election end Sánchez's rule and put Vox into government?
stories.dek: Polls say it could happen, but it is not certain. If the conservative PP and the hard-right Vox together win 176 of 350 seats, Vox could join the government. The hard right has not held power in Spain since 1975.

so_far.text: Pedro Sánchez of the Socialist party (PSOE) has led Spain since 2018. In a snap election in July 2023, no party reached the 176 of 350 seats needed for a majority. In November 2023 Sánchez stayed in power with votes from Catalan nationalists. In return, they got an amnesty for separatist leaders. Since then, corruption scandals have hurt him, and the hard-right party Vox has grown.

what_happened.text: Spain holds a snap general election on Sunday 29 November 2026. Sánchez called it early after protests over housing. Parliament had defeated two government bills to protect tenants from eviction, though his acting government later passed them. Polls lean to the right. An El País survey projected the PP and Vox together at 198 seats, above the 176 needed, with the PSOE at 112. An RTVE survey had Vox rising from 33 to 65 seats. The state-run pollster CIS is an outlier. It projects 155–171 seats for the PP and Vox combined.

steps.text: A Spanish prime minister needs 176 of 350 votes in parliament, so the biggest party alone often falls short.
El País projects the PP and Vox together at 198 seats, above 176, and the PSOE at only 112.
Vox would back PP leader Feijóo as prime minister only if it joins a coalition government in return.
Scandals and the Catalan amnesty have hurt Sánchez. Vox wants Spaniards put ahead of foreign residents. Sánchez is betting that housing matters more to voters.
If the PP and Vox pass 176 together, the hard right would hold national power for the first time since 1975.

history.text:
The story starts with Francisco Franco's dictatorship. It executed and persecuted rivals and abolished elections. Since Franco died in 1975, Spaniards have kept the far right out of national government. That is why Vox joining the government would be a first.

Vox was founded in December 2013, when it split from the conservative People's Party (PP). Santiago Abascal became its president in September 2014. At first it was tiny. It won only about 0.2% of the vote in the 2015 and 2016 general elections.

Its breakthrough came in December 2018, when it won 12 seats in Andalusia's regional election. By November 2019 it had 52 seats in Congress and was the third-largest party.

From March 2022 Vox joined PP-led regional governments as the junior partner. Castile and León came first. Valencia, Extremadura and Aragon followed after May 2023. So the two parties got used to governing together in the regions.

On 29 May 2023 Sánchez called a snap election, held on 23 July. The PP won 137 seats, the PSOE 121 and Vox 33. No party had 176. Feijóo failed to win parliament's vote. On 16 November 2023 Sánchez was re-elected with Catalan nationalist help. In return they got an amnesty bill, and the amnesty angered many voters.

In July 2024 Vox quit PP coalitions in five regions over asylum decisions for undocumented underage migrants. Even so, it doubled its seats in snap elections in Extremadura (December 2025) and Aragon (February 2026). The PP now relies on it there. In May 2026 police entered Socialist headquarters as part of a corruption probe.

France's National Rally also aims to take power in its next election.

misconception.myth: The party that wins the most seats automatically forms Spain's government.
misconception.fact: A prime minister needs parliament's backing. In 2023 the PP won the most seats (137), but Feijóo failed to win the vote. Sánchez was re-elected with support from smaller parties.

scenes.say: Sunday, 29 November 2026 ko Spain mein snap election hai. Kya isse Pedro Sanchez ka raaj khatam ho sakta hai, jo 2018 mein shuru hua tha? Aur kya hard-right party Vox government mein aa sakti hai? Spain mein hard right 1975 ke baad se kabhi power mein nahi raha.
scenes.show: Spain votes 29 November: is Sánchez out?
scenes.speak: Sunday, 29 November 2026 को Spain में snap election है। क्या इससे Pedro Sanchez का राज ख़त्म हो सकता है, जो 2018 में शुरू हुआ था? और क्या hard-right party Vox government में आ सकती है? Spain में hard right 1975 के बाद से कभी power में नहीं रहा।

scenes.say: Sanchez ne yeh early vote housing par protests ke baad bulaya. Parliament ne unki government ke 2 bills gira diye the, jo tenants ko eviction se bachane ke liye the. Baad mein unki acting government ne unhe pass kar diya. Unki ummeed hai ki voters ke liye housing ka gussa baaki shikayaton se zyada maayne rakhega.
scenes.show: Housing protests led to the early vote
scenes.speak: Sanchez ने यह early vote housing पर protests के बाद बुलाया। Parliament ने उनकी government के 2 bills गिरा दिए थे, जो tenants को eviction से बचाने के लिए थे। बाद में उनकी acting government ने उन्हें pass कर दिया। उनकी उम्मीद है कि voters के लिए housing का गुस्सा बाकी शिकायतों से ज़्यादा मायने रखेगा।

scenes.say: Polls right ki taraf jhuke hain. El Pais ke ek survey ke projection mein conservative People's Party aur Vox milakar 198 seats par hain. Majority ke liye 176 chahiye. Usi mein Sanchez ke Socialists 112 par hain, jabki 2023 mein 121 the.
scenes.speak: Polls right की तरफ़ झुके हैं। El Pais के एक survey के projection में conservative People's Party और Vox मिलाकर 198 seats पर हैं। Majority के लिए 176 चाहिए। उसी में Sanchez के Socialists 112 पर हैं, जबकि 2023 में 121 थे।

scenes.say: Toh hum yahan tak pahunche kaise? Shuru karte hain Francisco Franco se. Unki dictatorship ne rivals ko execute kiya, unhe sataya, aur elections khatam kar diye. 1975 mein unki maut ke baad se Spain ke logon ne far right ko national government se bahar rakha hai. Young voters ko woh daur kam yaad hai.
scenes.speak: तो हम यहाँ तक पहुँचे कैसे? शुरू करते हैं Francisco Franco से। उनकी dictatorship ने rivals को execute किया, उन्हें सताया, और elections ख़त्म कर दिए। 1975 में उनकी मौत के बाद से Spain के लोगों ने far right को national government से बाहर रखा है। Young voters को वो दौर कम याद है।

scenes.say: Vox December 2013 mein bani, jab woh People's Party se alag hui. 2014 mein Santiago Abascal iske president bane. Shuru mein yeh bahut chhoti thi. 2015 aur 2016 mein ise sirf lagbhag zero point 2 percent vote mile.
scenes.speak: Vox December 2013 में बनी, जब वो People's Party से अलग हुई। 2014 में Santiago Abascal इसके president बने। शुरू में यह बहुत छोटी थी। 2015 और 2016 में इसे सिर्फ़ लगभग zero point 2 percent vote मिले।

scenes.say: Phir aaya breakthrough. December 2018 mein Vox ne Andalusia mein 12 seats jeeti. November 2019 tak Congress mein uske paas 52 seats thi, aur woh teesri sabse badi party ban gayi. March 2022 se woh regions mein People's Party governments mein junior partner ke taur par shaamil hone lagi.
scenes.speak: फिर आया breakthrough। December 2018 में Vox ने Andalusia में 12 seats जीतीं। November 2019 तक Congress में उसके पास 52 seats थीं, और वो तीसरी सबसे बड़ी party बन गई। March 2022 से वो regions में People's Party governments में junior partner के तौर पर शामिल होने लगी।

scenes.say: 29 May 2023 ko Sanchez ne 23 July ke liye snap election bulaya. People's Party ko 137 seats mili, Socialists ko 121, aur Vox ko 33. Kisi party ke paas 176 nahi the. Feijoo parliament ka vote nahi jeet paaye. November 2023 mein Sanchez Catalan nationalists ke votes se dobara chune gaye. Badle mein unhe amnesty mili.
scenes.show: 2023: no majority, then an amnesty deal
scenes.speak: 29 May 2023 को Sanchez ने 23 July के लिए snap election बुलाया। People's Party को 137 seats मिलीं, Socialists को 121, और Vox को 33। किसी party के पास 176 नहीं थे। Feijoo parliament का vote नहीं जीत पाए। November 2023 में Sanchez Catalan nationalists के votes से दोबारा चुने गए। बदले में उन्हें amnesty मिली।

scenes.say: Uske baad se pressure badhta gaya. July 2024 mein Vox migrant bachchon ke mudde par 5 regions mein People's Party governments se bahar nikal gayi. Phir bhi December 2025 mein Extremadura aur February 2026 mein Aragon ke snap elections mein uski seats double ho gayi. Ab wahan People's Party ko uska sahara chahiye.
scenes.show: Vox doubled its seats in two regions
scenes.speak: उसके बाद से pressure बढ़ता गया। July 2024 में Vox migrant बच्चों के मुद्दे पर 5 regions में People's Party governments से बाहर निकल गई। फिर भी December 2025 में Extremadura और February 2026 में Aragon के snap elections में उसकी seats double हो गईं। अब वहाँ People's Party को उसका सहारा चाहिए।

scenes.say: Toh Sanchez haar kyun sakte hain? Unki family se jude scandals ne government ko nuksaan pahunchaya hai. May 2026 mein ek corruption probe mein police Socialist headquarters mein ghusi. Catalan amnesty se kai voters naraz hue. Vox chahti hai ki Spain ke logon ko foreign residents se pehle rakha jaye. Sanchez ka daav hai ki housing ki chinta immigration ke dar se zyada maayne rakhegi.
scenes.speak: तो Sanchez हार क्यों सकते हैं? उनकी family से जुड़े scandals ने government को नुकसान पहुँचाया है। May 2026 में एक corruption probe में police Socialist headquarters में घुसी। Catalan amnesty से कई voters नाराज़ हुए। Vox चाहती है कि Spain के लोगों को foreign residents से पहले रखा जाए। Sanchez का दाँव है कि housing की चिंता immigration के डर से ज़्यादा मायने रखेगी।

scenes.say: Aur Vox government mein kyun aa sakti hai? Prime minister banne ke liye 350 mein se 176 votes chahiye. El Pais People's Party aur Vox ko milakar 198 par rakhta hai, aur Socialists ko 112 par. Vox kehti hai ki woh Feijoo ka saath degi, lekin sirf tab jab use government mein jagah mile. Aisa hua toh 1975 ke baad pehli baar hoga.
scenes.show: Vox's price: a place in government
scenes.speak: और Vox government में क्यों आ सकती है? Prime minister बनने के लिए 350 में से 176 votes चाहिए। El Pais People's Party और Vox को मिलाकर 198 पर रखता है, और Socialists को 112 पर। Vox कहती है कि वो Feijoo का साथ देगी, लेकिन सिर्फ़ तब जब उसे government में जगह मिले। ऐसा हुआ तो 1975 के बाद पहली बार होगा।

scenes.say: Ab players ki baat. Pedro Sanchez Socialists ke leader hain aur 2018 se prime minister hain. Alberto Nunez Feijoo People's Party ke leader aur main challenger hain. Santiago Abascal Vox ko lead karte hain. Aur Catalan party Junts ne 2023 mein Sanchez ko dobara chunne mein madad ki thi.
scenes.speak: अब players की बात। Pedro Sanchez Socialists के leader हैं और 2018 से prime minister हैं। Alberto Nunez Feijoo People's Party के leader और main challenger हैं। Santiago Abascal Vox को lead करते हैं। और Catalan party Junts ने 2023 में Sanchez को दोबारा चुनने में मदद की थी।

scenes.say: Congress mein Vox ki seats dekhiye. April 2019 mein 24. November 2019 mein 52. 2023 mein ghatkar 33. Ab RTVE ka ek survey 65 ka projection deta hai, lagbhag double. Isiliye Vox kingmaker ban sakti hai.
scenes.speak: Congress में Vox की seats देखिए। April 2019 में 24। November 2019 में 52। 2023 में घटकर 33। अब RTVE का एक survey 65 का projection देता है, लगभग double। इसीलिए Vox kingmaker बन सकती है।

scenes.say: Har poll ek jaisa nahi kehta. Ek poll mein People's Party 29 point 5 percent par thi aur Socialists 27 point 2 par. Sarkari pollster CIS baaki sab se alag hai. Woh People's Party aur Vox ko milakar sirf 155 se 171 seats deta hai.
scenes.speak: हर poll एक जैसा नहीं कहता। एक poll में People's Party 29 point 5 percent पर थी और Socialists 27 point 2 पर। सरकारी pollster CIS बाकी सब से अलग है। वो People's Party और Vox को मिलाकर सिर्फ़ 155 से 171 seats देता है।

scenes.say: Ab asli idea: Spain apna prime minister kaise chunta hai. Voters 350 deputies chunte hain, prime minister nahi. Phir deputies ek investiture vote karte hain ki lead kaun karega. Pehla vote jeetne ke liye candidate ko 176 chahiye. Sabse zyada seats jeetna kaafi nahi hai. Feijoo ne yeh 2023 mein seekha.
scenes.speak: अब असली idea: Spain अपना prime minister कैसे चुनता है। Voters 350 deputies चुनते हैं, prime minister नहीं। फिर deputies एक investiture vote करते हैं कि lead कौन करेगा। पहला vote जीतने के लिए candidate को 176 चाहिए। सबसे ज़्यादा seats जीतना काफ़ी नहीं है। Feijoo ने यह 2023 में सीखा।

scenes.say: Agar kisi party ke paas 176 nahi hain, toh use partners chahiye. Coalition mein partners ministries aapas mein baantte hain. Kingmaker ek chhoti party hoti hai jiski seats kisi badi party ko line ke paar pahuncha deti hain. Woh apni keemat maang sakti hai. Agar pehla vote fail ho jaye, toh dusre vote mein bas no se zyada yes votes chahiye.
scenes.show: Kingmaker: the small party that decides
scenes.speak: अगर किसी party के पास 176 नहीं हैं, तो उसे partners चाहिए। Coalition में partners ministries आपस में बाँटते हैं। Kingmaker एक छोटी party होती है जिसकी seats किसी बड़ी party को line के पार पहुँचा देती हैं। वो अपनी कीमत माँग सकती है। अगर पहला vote fail हो जाए, तो दूसरे vote में बस no से ज़्यादा yes votes चाहिए।

scenes.say: Chaliye ek example lete hain. Maan lijiye parliament mein 350 seats hain. Majority hai 176. Party A ne 140 jeeti. Saari 35 small-party seats jod dijiye, toh ho gaye 175. Bas ek kam. Uski rival, Party C, madad nahi karegi. Lekin Party B ke paas 60 hain. A aur B milke 200. Toh Party B hai kingmaker.
scenes.speak: चलिए एक example लेते हैं। मान लीजिए parliament में 350 seats हैं। Majority है 176। Party A ने 140 जीतीं। सारी 35 small-party seats जोड़ दीजिए, तो हो गए 175। बस एक कम। उसकी rival, Party C, मदद नहीं करेगी। लेकिन Party B के पास 60 हैं। A और B मिलके 200। तो Party B है kingmaker।

scenes.say: Ab views. Sanchez chetavni dete hain ki Vox wali People's Party government koi aam government nahi hogi. Unke mutabik Vox abortion, euthanasia aur green energy policies ko nishana banayegi. Abascal far-right label ko nakaarte hain. Woh Vox ki positions ko common sense kehte hain.
scenes.speak: अब views। Sanchez चेतावनी देते हैं कि Vox वाली People's Party government कोई आम government नहीं होगी। उनके मुताबिक Vox abortion, euthanasia और green energy policies को निशाना बनाएगी। Abascal far-right label को नकारते हैं। वो Vox की positions को common sense कहते हैं।

Vox's positions are 'common sense', not far right

scenes.say: Feijoo is vote ko corruption aur decency banaam decline aur prosperity ki ladai batate hain. Political scientist Steven Forti kehte hain ki People's Party aur Vox ki government poore Europe mein far right ko normal banane ki taraf ek aur kadam hogi.
scenes.speak: Feijoo इस vote को corruption और decency बनाम decline और prosperity की लड़ाई बताते हैं। Political scientist Steven Forti कहते हैं कि People's Party और Vox की government पूरे Europe में far right को normal बनाने की तरफ़ एक और कदम होगी।

scenes.say: India mein aapke liye iska kya matlab hai? Seedhe taur par, bahut kam. Yahan prices, jobs aur rules nahi badalte. Lekin yeh ek signal hai. Vox ka rise France ki National Rally jaisa hai, jo France ke agle election mein power lena chahti hai.
scenes.speak: India में आपके लिए इसका क्या मतलब है? सीधे तौर पर, बहुत कम। यहाँ prices, jobs और rules नहीं बदलते। लेकिन यह एक signal है। Vox का rise France की National Rally जैसा है, जो France के अगले election में power लेना चाहती है।

scenes.say: Ek aam galti hai yeh sochna ki sabse badi party apne aap government banati hai. Aisa nahi hai. Ab hamara lesson lagaiye. Agar right ko 198 seats milti hain, toh Vox kingmaker hai aur government mein jagah maang sakti hai. Agar sirf 155 se 171 milti hain, toh chhoti parties phir se faisla karengi, jaise 2023 mein.
scenes.show: Biggest party does not automatically govern

stories.headline: US licence rule tightens Chinese AI labs' access to rented chips
stories.question: How does a new US rule limit Chinese AI labs renting chips abroad?
stories.dek: A US rule effective 19 November makes Chinese firms get licences to rent large US-chip computing abroad. Nvidia reportedly halted servers to four Southeast Asian countries, and Chinese AI launches may slip.

so_far.text: Since October 2022 the US has limited which advanced chips can be sold to China. Some Chinese firms, such as Moonshot AI, rent computing power in data centres abroad instead. On 16 November the US Commerce Department announced a rule, effective 19 November. It requires licences for advanced chips sent to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. It also requires licences for Chinese firms to use large amounts of US-chip computing in overseas data centres. US-headquartered customers are excluded but must file reports. Operators already serving Chinese firms have 90 days to get licences.

what_happened.text: On 26 November the Financial Times reported that Nvidia asked its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers with its AI chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. Server makers Dell and Supermicro told customers there that Nvidia would not authorise their orders. It is unclear whether the halt is temporary. Reuters could not verify the report, and none of the three companies gave an immediate response. The same day CNBC reported that buyers of Nvidia chips are being told to rule out Chinese renters. Reuters reported that two Chinese labs, Z.AI and Moonshot AI, face delays to their next big models.

steps.text: US rules since October 2022 stop the most advanced US chips from being sold into China.
But a Chinese lab does not need to own chips; it can rent them in data centres abroad.
The 16 November rule requires licences for Chinese firms using large compute, about 750 H100-equivalents, in overseas data centres.
After the rule, the FT reported Nvidia paused AI servers to four countries; CNBC says buyers must exclude Chinese renters.
With less rented compute, Chinese labs train more slowly, so Z.AI's GLM-5.5 and Moonshot's Kimi K4 could slip into 2027.

history.text:
It began in October 2022, when Washington first restricted exports of high-end chips to China on national-security grounds. In December 2022 it blacklisted 36 Chinese firms. In October 2023 it widened the curbs to lower-performing Nvidia chips, and Nvidia built a cut-down chip for China, the H20. Sales of the H20 then swung back and forth. Licences were required in April 2025. In July 2025 Nvidia said it would resume sales after Washington removed those curbs.

In January 2025 China's DeepSeek chatbot topped Apple's US download charts. That showed Chinese labs could compete despite the curbs. The same month, Biden's AI Diffusion Rule would have capped advanced AI chip sales worldwide. The Trump administration withdrew it in mid-2025 for a more calibrated approach, but did not loosen curbs on China.

By 2026 attention turned to two workarounds. The first is distillation, which means training a model on a stronger model's answers. Anthropic had alleged over 16 million Claude interactions through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts. In September 2026 it reported nearly 200 million exchanges linked to suspected distillation. The second workaround is renting chips in data centres abroad. The 16 November 2026 rule targets that route directly.

lesson.concept: How a compute threshold decides who needs a licence
lesson.big_idea: AI labs don't need to own chips; they can rent computing power in data centres abroad. The new US rule counts how much a Chinese firm rents. Above a set level, it needs a licence.

steps.title: Compute is the chips' work
steps.text: Training an AI model needs huge amounts of compute: the calculations done by AI chips. It is often counted in H100-equivalents, meaning how many of Nvidia's H100 chips the work would take.

steps.title: Compute can be rented
steps.text: A data centre owns the chips and rents their time over the internet. A lab in Beijing can train on chips in Malaysia that never enter China. Moonshot AI, for example, prioritises overseas providers.

steps.title: Old curbs watched shipments
steps.text: Since October 2022, US rules have limited which high-end chips can be sold to China. These rules focus on where chips are shipped, which left the rented route open.

steps.title: The new rule counts renters
steps.text: From 19 November, Chinese firms need a licence to use large compute, about 750 H100-equivalents, from advanced US chips in overseas data centres. Operators already serving them have 90 days to get licences.

steps.title: A licence is a gate
steps.text: A licence is not a ban: the US government decides each case, and big rentals wait for its answer. Meanwhile, CNBC reported that buyers of Nvidia chips are being told to rule out Chinese renters.

example.result: The rule doesn't stop a lab using a little compute; it stops a big lab renting lots abroad without permission. A data centre relying on big Chinese renters could lose half its business.

practice.q: A Thai data centre already rents 900 H100-equivalents to one Chinese lab and 400 to another. Which deal needs a licence, and by when?
practice.answer: Compare each with about 750. First deal: 900 is above 750, so it needs a licence. Second deal: 400 is below 750, so assume it does not. The centre already serves the lab, so it has 90 days from 19 November: about 17 February 2027.

Lab B ko 300 chahiye. Line se neeche, toh maan lete hain licence nahi chahiye. Agar Lab A ko mana ho gaya, toh aadha centre khaali padا rahega.
scenes.speak: चलिए एक example देखते हैं। मान लीजिए Malaysia में एक data centre है, 2000 H100-equivalents का। Lab A को 1000 चाहिए। यह 750 से ऊपर है, तो licence चाहिए। Lab B को 300 चाहिए। Line से नीचे, तो मान लेते हैं licence नहीं चाहिए। अगर Lab A को मना हो गया, तो आधा centre खाली पड़ा रहेगा।

scenes.say: Ab ghadi jodiye. 19 November se 90 din, yaani lagbhag 17 February 2027 tak. Asli data centres ke saamne yahi situation hai. Lab A ki tarah bade Chinese renters licence ke gate par khade hain, aur lenders aur buyers peeche hat rahe hain.
scenes.speak: अब घड़ी जोड़िए। 19 November से 90 दिन, यानी लगभग 17 February 2027 तक। असली data centres के सामने यही situation है। Lab A की तरह बड़े Chinese renters licence के gate पर खड़े हैं, और lenders और buyers पीछे हट रहे हैं।

scenes.say: Raay alag alag hai. Anthropic kehta hai Alibaba, Moonshot aur Z.AI ne Claude ko distill kiya, lagbhag 200 million exchanges, aur chip limits iska scale kam karti hain. Moonshot distillation se inkaar karti hai. Ek cloud executive ne Financial Times se kaha, yeh poora chaos hai. 90 din ki ghadi chal rahi hai aur kisi ko nahi pata apply kaise karein.
scenes.speak: राय अलग अलग है। Anthropic कहता है Alibaba, Moonshot और Z.AI ने Claude को distill किया, लगभग 200 million exchanges, और chip limits इसका scale कम करती हैं। Moonshot distillation से इनकार करती है। एक cloud executive ने Financial Times से कहा, यह पूरा chaos है। 90 दिन की घड़ी चल रही है और किसी को नहीं पता apply कैसे करें।

scenes.say: Ek aam galatfehmi: yeh sochna ki export curbs tabhi lagte hain jab chips China mein ship hoti hain. Yeh rule un Chinese firms par bhi lagta hai jo overseas data centres mein, jaise Malaysia mein, bada compute rent karti hain.
scenes.speak: एक आम ग़लतफ़हमी: यह सोचना कि export curbs तभी लगते हैं जब chips China में ship होती हैं। यह rule उन Chinese firms पर भी लगता है जो overseas data centres में, जैसे Malaysia में, बड़ा compute rent करती हैं।

scenes.say: India ke liye iska kya matlab hai? Rule mein jo 5 desh hain, unmein India nahi hai. In reports mein Indian users, prices ya apps par koi seedha asar nahi bataya gaya. Phir bhi baat ahem hai. Yeh dikhata hai ki US curbs China ke bahar ke data centres tak pahunch sakte hain, jaise Malaysia ke. Aur hamare example ki tarah, wahan bade Chinese renters licence gate ka saamna karte hain.
scenes.show: India not on the rule's list
scenes.speak: India के लिए इसका क्या मतलब है? Rule में जो 5 देश हैं, उनमें India नहीं है। इन reports में Indian users, prices या apps पर कोई सीधा असर नहीं बताया गया। फिर भी बात अहम है। यह दिखाता है कि US curbs China के बाहर के data centres तक पहुँच सकते हैं, जैसे Malaysia के। और हमारे example की तरह, वहाँ बड़े Chinese renters licence gate का सामना करते हैं।

scenes.say: Aage kya? 90 din ki licence deadline par nazar rakhiye, lagbhag 17 February 2027. Aur dekhiye ki Nvidia rok ko confirm karti hai ya koi end date deti hai. Abhi pata nahi ki Commerce Department licences kaise process karega, aur kitne Southeast Asian projects in servers par tike hain.
scenes.speak: आगे क्या? 90 दिन की licence deadline पर नज़र रखिए, लगभग 17 February 2027। और देखिए कि Nvidia रोक को confirm करती है या कोई end date देती है। अभी पता नहीं कि Commerce Department licences कैसे process करेगा, और कितने Southeast Asian projects इन servers पर टिके हैं।

scenes.say: Toh teen baatein yaad rakhiye. Chinese labs videsh mein US chips rent karti hain, aur naye rule mein lagbhag 750 H100-equivalents se upar licence chahiye. Nvidia ne kathit taur par 4 deshon ko servers roke, aur Chinese AI launches khisak sakte hain. Aur licence deadline par nazar rakhiye, lagbhag 17 February 2027.
scenes.speak: तो तीन बातें याद रखिए। Chinese labs विदेश में US chips rent करती हैं, और नए rule में लगभग 750 H100-equivalents से ऊपर licence चाहिए। Nvidia ने कथित तौर पर 4 देशों को servers रोके, और Chinese AI launches खिसक सकते हैं। और licence deadline पर नज़र रखिए, लगभग 17 February 2027।

It grows by 50%
It shrinks for states with slower population growth

quiz.q: If India signs the deal, what happens to its US tariff compared with the 10% baseline of 27 November 2026?
options: It falls below 10%
It rises from 10% to 17%, instead of to 25%
It stays at 10%
quiz.why: The baseline on 27 November 2026 is 10%. The proposal replaces it with 25%, or 17% with a deal. A deal limits the rise; it doesn't cut the rate.

quiz.q: Why might SAP accept a large one-time cost to cut roles?
options: The salary savings repeat every year and repay the cost over time
A one-time cost brings the yearly salary bill down to zero
Cutting roles raises sales straight away
quiz.why: Exit pay and retraining are paid once, but saved salaries recur every year, so the cut pays for itself after the payback period.
